lines.text: A website goes down. Before any official statement, people are already posting about it. Can a machine hear that?
lines.source: Ural and Acarturk 2021, Sec. 1.1 (an attack on a site is reported by social media users first)

lines.text: The trouble is the flood. Millions of ordinary posts, and somewhere in them, a handful about a real attack.
lines.source: Sec. 1.1, 4.4 (millions of documents a day; most posts are not informative)

lines.text: In Turkish, there was no ready-made collection of examples to learn from. So we started from one attack whose answer we already knew.
lines.source: Sec. 1.1, 2.2 (no Turkish data set or term dictionary; one past incident, the nic.tr attack, used as the reference)

lines.text: December 2015: Turkey's domain servers are attacked. We compared what people wrote in the year before, on the day, and in the two weeks after. The words that stood out became our vocabulary.
lines.source: Sec. 2.2, 4.1 (three databases: the year before, the attack day, the two weeks after; TF-IDF)

lines.text: Then every word had to earn its place. If it brought more false alarms than real detections, it was out.
lines.source: Sec. 2.2 (A/B test: a keyword that raises false positives is not added)

lines.text: Too many words, and the analyst drowns in false alarms. Too few, and the attack is noticed late. So we set the bar in advance: catch it on the day, with fewer than one false alarm in three.
lines.source: Sec. 4.1, 4.4 (too many keywords lower certainty, too few lower sensitivity; criteria: detect on the attack day, no more than 30 percent false positives)

lines.text: Posts are messy, and Turkish packs a lot into one word. So the text is cleaned up first: many spellings, one word.
lines.source: Sec. 2.3 (every text is normalised through the ITU Turkish NLP service before detection)

lines.text: Then the detector does something simple. It doesn't try to understand the posts. It counts how often each possible target is named, day by day, and waits for a day that doesn't look like the others.
lines.source: Sec. 2.1, 2.3 (a vector of possible victims; daily mention counts against a threshold from the entity's own history)

lines.text: On the day of the attack, the count for the target jumped. That jump was the alarm.
lines.source: Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2 (the attack is detected on its first day)

lines.text: In a test run, about three alarms in four were real. And we published the false ones too, like a post that only asked: was your account hacked?
lines.source: Sec. 4.3.1, 4.4 (437 entries, 29 detections, 22 positive, 7 false; the 'hacklendi' false positive)

lines.text: Because it reads Turkish, it caught incidents that a tool built for English would have missed.
lines.source: Sec. 4.2.2 (an incident published in Turkish, which a system reading English text could not detect)

lines.text: Most of the world doesn't write in English. A tool that listens only in English is deaf to most of it.
